builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Item Representations Matter: Bridging Hard Semantic IDs and Soft Prototype Mixtures for Generative Retrieval
summary: It replaces flat per-item embedding tables and hard quantized Semantic IDs in generative retrieval recommenders with a soft mixture of shared prototypes plus an item-specific residual vector, trained jointly and kept continuous at inference. It costs the additional prototype and assignment parameters, joint training complexity, and tuning of assignment priors, though it avoids a separate quantization tokenizer and can improve inference throughput relative to discrete code decoding. Gains are concentrated on sparse datasets (two Amazon benchmarks) with only a small improvement on Steam, so on dense or well-populated item catalogs the added machinery may not pay off, and pretrained content embeddings or SID priors are needed for the stronger configurations.
rationale: The method targets recommender retrieval rather than LLM inference, but it is small-scale and single-GPU feasible, so a team running sequential recommendation workloads should validate it on their own data before adopting.
technique: Soft prototype-mixture item embeddings for generative recommendation

claims.statement: It replaces flat per-item embedding tables and hard quantized Semantic IDs in generative retrieval recommenders with a soft mixture of shared prototypes plus an item-specific residual vector, trained jointly and kept continuous at inference. It costs the additional prototype and assignment parameters, joint training complexity, and tuning of assignment priors, though it avoids a separate quantization tokenizer and can improve inference throughput relative to discrete code decoding. Gains are concentrated on sparse datasets (two Amazon benchmarks) with only a small improvement on Steam, so on dense or well-populated item catalogs the added machinery may not pay off, and pretrained content embeddings or SID priors are needed for the stronger configurations.

CAP-Mix improves HR@5 and NDCG@5 by 6.9% and 13.6% relative to the best baseline averaged across six benchmarks, beats a hard Semantic-ID table from the same tokenizer by 4.45-14.90% in HR@5, and delivers 1.4-161x the inference throughput of the discrete baselines.
